title: Find the best place to work
author: Franck Pachot
body_html:
The previous post was about consulting from the point of view of the customer. I mentioned that the consultants must not be 100% at customers. They must build their practices, knowledge, and skills continuously. Then, if you are going to be a consultant, the choice of your employer is extremely important. Here are a few recommendations, from my experience, for people looking for a job in IT, especially as a consultant.

The interview. This is probably not specific to IT but, with those companies, I did only a few interviews with people for which interviewing candidates was actually their job. Consulting companies may not have a large Human Resource department. And then I had 2 kinds of interviews. One kind is the interview with the commercial manager, in companies for which the main goal is to place engineers full time at customers. That's not easy because they don't really understand your technical skills, and you are probably not comfortable trying to sell your skills with someone who is a salesperson himself. I have seen, on multiple occasions, the interviewer trying to undervalue your competencies, with the idea to lower your salary expectation at the end. Clearly avoid those ones: it can only get worse once you will work for them.

More interesting are the interviews with technical people. Probably easier because there are many points where you admire what they did, like when they evolved when from consultant to CEO. And they also have many points where they admire you because you have the skills they are lacking, and for which they are looking for new candidates. And you can share your common history in IT, which is an easier context for showing how you approach the problems.

I was really impressed by an interview once, where the CEO and the CTO started to talk about themselves and their company before asking questions. How they came to create the company, and how they are enthusiastic about their product, and confident in the future. When the interview starts with the feeling that they want to convince you to work for them, you start in the best mood.

But there's a catch when the interviewer is not an HR specialist: the evaluation is very subjective and can be easily biased. Here is an interesting read: https://www.socialtalent.com/blog/diversity-and-inclusion/9-types-of-bias. CoakroachDB has detailed how they conduct interviews, trying to fight those biases: https://www.cockroachlabs.com/blog/fighting-unconscious-bias-cockroach-labs/. On one hand, subjectivity is not bad because in the end you will work together and then the first feeling must be good. But on the other hand, those biases may let you completely miss some important points, negative or positive, on both sides.

In summary: be confident and go to an interview where each party tries to see the best from the other. If it is not the case, then it cannot be a good start. If you want to work in a great place, the interview must be an awesome experience.

The truth. That's the most important for both sides in a recruitment interview: do not lie, do not hide anything. If you feel some negative aspects: talk about them and you will see if it is something that can be improved. But hiding the dust under the carpet is not sustainable. The problems will arise and solutions will be harder to find when people feel that they were fooled.

Surveys. There are companies who know that happy people will do their best. and some apply to Great Place to Work. This means that a survey is conducted by an external company to get feedback from the employees on many topics.

But I've also seen a company that conducted a similar survey. When they presented the results, someone asked about what will be attempted to improve the weak areas. The answer was something like: you will always have people happy and people unhappy, so do not expect major changes...

Between those two extremes, I immediately know where I want to work. The best place is probably where there's a synergy of people always trying to improve. The management tries to improve wellness, the consultants try to improve their achievements, and all can go for the best satisfaction.

Those 'Great Place to Work' labels and reputations are important. A company doing this effort shows the importance they put on it. Like yourself when you pass technical certifications to prove that you have some skills and that you always want to raise the level. One label by itself may not be significant, but two awards showing improvement, this is a proof of caring about the employee's wellness.

Trust. There are companies who are reluctant to give you training. They think that if your skills improve, then you will either ask for a higher salary, or you will leave. That may be right, but holding the employees at a low level is just killing the business. A good consulting company will help you to gain more skills, experience, and recognition. And you will stay in this company because of the previous point about wellness: you will not leave the best place to work.

Finally, juniors may hesitate between consulting of fixed position. I see a lot of advantages of being a consultant when starting in IT. Always learning, ready for the next technology. And always prepared for changes. If you focus more on a career evolution to management, then a fixed position may be preferable. Also, big challenges may need high involvement (time, travels, workload). Be sure to keep the right balance between work and private life. The balance may change during the personal lifecycle (couple, kids, family,..) and a good company should know that.

Here is probably the last post of this small series that I wanted to write while being temporary out of consulting business, for better objectivity. I'll be back as a consultant soon - and for sure in a great place to work. Do not hesitate to get in touch for any feedback, comment or question. The best way for this is Twitter: @FranckPachot
